query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) based on the W–Ta–Cr–V system (with potential minor alloying such as Hf) can serve as an effective interlayer between tungsten (W) and CuCrZr in nuclear fusion reactor applications because its intermediate thermal expansion behavior and high radiation/thermal stability can mitigate thermal stresses and bonding issues.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk tungsten (a high-melting, brittle plasma-facing material) and CuCrZr (a high thermal conductivity heat sink alloy) that have substantially different coefficients of thermal expansion and irradiation responses.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin, continuous coating or layer of the W–Ta–Cr–V-based refractory HEA between the W and CuCrZr components via an appropriate deposition or sintering process.
generation.conditions: Service conditions relevant to fusion reactors, including high temperature, intense thermal cycling, and exposure to high-energy neutron and ion irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: The single-phase, nanocrystalline structure of the HEA which provides an intermediate coefficient of thermal expansion and strong metallurgical bonding with both W and CuCrZr.
generation.mechanism: The HEA interlayer is expected to reduce thermal mismatch stress by acting as a graded buffer. Its inherent radiation resistance and high-temperature stability help maintain cohesive bonding under cyclic thermal loads and irradiation, thereby preventing interfacial cracking and degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite system with the HEA interlayer will exhibit improved interfacial integrity, reduced microcracking during thermal cycling, and enhanced durability under irradiation compared to a direct W/CuCrZr bond.
generation.baseline: Directly bonding W to CuCrZr, which typically suffers from high residual stresses, poor adhesion, and early interfacial failure due to the large mismatch in thermal expansion properties.
generation.boundary: This approach may be sensitive to processing parameters (e.g., interlayer thickness, deposition method) and potential diffusion at the interfaces over long exposure times; precise optimization is needed to avoid degradation.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative benefits are supported by observations of HEA properties in related studies, precisely quantifying the thermal expansion matching and long-term irradiation effects requires further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of joined samples: one with a direct W/CuCrZr interface and one with an inserted W–Ta–Cr–V-based HEA interlayer. Subject both sets to cyclic thermal loading and simulated irradiation conditions that mimic fusion reactor operation.
measurements: Quantitative bond strength testing at room and elevated temperatures
Interfacial microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM/TEM) to detect cracking or delamination
Thermal expansion coefficient measurements of the interlayer and adjacent materials
Irradiation damage assessments via ion beam exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the HEA interlayer do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in interfacial cracking, improved bond strength, and better endurance under thermal cycling and irradiation compared to direct W/CuCrZr joints, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations
